#### REVOLT OF 1857

#### PRE-1857 REVOLTS

Reasons for Land Revolts in India

  • Before Independence, there were three major land reforms prevailing in the country:
  1. 1. Permanent Settlement
  2. 2. Ryotwari System
  3. 3. Mahalwari System
Lord Cornwallis introduced Daroga System replacing Zamindari Thanedars.

Permanent Settlement (1793)

  • Introduced by: Lord Cornwallis.
  • It is also known as "Zamindari System".
  • Under the Zamindari system, the land revenue was collected from the farmers by the intermediaries known as Zamindars (the middle man).
  • It was introduced in: Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh.
A sunset clause was introduced in the Zamindari system that required zamindars to pay a fixed amount of revenue by a specific date, before sunset. If the zamindars failed to pay the revenue on time, the government would confiscate and auction off their zamindari, which was hereditary.

Ryotwari System (1820)

  • Introduced by: Munro and Reed.
  • It was based on Ricardian Theory of Rent.
  • Under the Ryotwari system (Ryot: Peasant), the land revenue was paid by the farmers directly to the state.
  • It was introduced in: South India (Madras region of Tamil Nadu).

Mahalwari System (1822)

  • Introduced by: Holt Mackenzie in Punjab and Northwestern province.
  • Under the Mahalwari system, the land revenue was collected from the farmers by the village headmen on behalf of the whole village (and not the zamindar).
  • The village or group of villages was termed a "Mahal" and treated as a single revenue unit.

#### REVOLTS

Sanyasi Revolt (1763)

  • It started in Bihar and Bengal.
  • Leaders: Majnu Shah, Bhawani Pathak, and Debi Chaudhurani (female participant).
  • Governor-General Warren Hastings faced the persistent Sanyasi and Faqir disturbances in Bengal and Bihar.
  • Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel "Anand Math" mentions about Sanyasi Rebellion of 1763.

Paika Revolt (1817)

  • It started in Odisha.
  • Leaders: Bakshi Jagbandhu Bidyadhar (Military Commander of Khurda kingdom).

Pagal Panthis (1825)

  • It started in Bengal region.
  • Leaders: Karam Shah and Tipu Shah.

Ahom Revolt (1828)

  • It started in Assam.
  • Leaders: Gomdhar Konwar.

Battle of Saraighat (1671)

  • It was fought between: Mughals and Ahom Kingdom.
  • The Ahom forces was led by Lachit Borphukan and the Mughal forces were led by Ram Singh.
  • Mughals were defeated.

Kol Mutiny (1831)

  • Leaders: Budho Bhagat.

Moplah Uprising (1836)

  • It started in Malabar region.

Ho and Munda Uprising (1820 and 1837)

  • It started in Ranchi and Singhbhum.
  • This revolt was fuelled by resentment against "Dikus" (outsiders).
  • The arrival of Dikus and the introduction of colonial land revenue system posed a direct threat to the Khuntkatti System (collective ownership).
  • Note: This is distinct from the later Ulgulan (1899-1900) led by Birsa Munda, which is also sometimes called the "Munda Uprising".
  • Birsa Munda — Birth: 15 Nov 1875 (celebrated as Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas and Jharkhand Foundation Day).
  • Death: 9 June 1900.

Gadkari Uprising (1844)

  • It started in Kolhapur.

Santhal Rebellion (1855)

  • It started in Damini-e-Koh, a large tract of forested hilly land in the Jharkhand region particularly around the Rajmahal Hills demarcated in 1832.
  • This large area of land was demarcated and declared to be the land of the Santhals (Santhal is the 3rd largest tribe in India).
  • Leaders: Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu.

Indigo Revolt (1859)

  • It started in Nadia (District) of Bengal.
  • Leaders: Digambar Biswas and Bishnucharan Biswas.
  • It was against the exploitative practices of British planters who forced Indian farmers to cultivate indigo instead of food crops on their land.
  • It was a successful revolt.
  • Dinbandhu Mitra wrote "Nil Darpan" (a play about Indigo Revolt).

#### 1857 REVOLT

Causes of 1857 Revolt

British Policies

  1. 1. General Service Establishment Act
  • Lord Canning brought this Act that mandated Indian soldiers of the Bengal Army to be sent overseas for duty.

#### REVOLT OF 1857

  1. 2. Doctrine of Lapse
  • It was introduced by Lord Dalhousie in 1848.
  • If an Indian ruler died without a male heir, his kingdom would "lapse" and automatically become part of the East India Company's territories.

Acquired places under Doctrine of Lapse:

  1. 1. Satara: 1848
  2. 2. Sambalpur, Jaitpur: 1849
  3. 3. Udaipur: 1852
  4. 4. Jhansi: 1853
  5. 5. Nagpur: 1854
- Dalhousie stated that "Awadh is like that cherry that will drop into our mouth one day".
- Awadh was captured on the grounds of Misgovernance.
- Mirza Wajid Ali Shah was the last Nawab of Awadh.

Sepoy Mutiny

  • Introduction of "Enfield" rifle: It was said that the cartridge of the rifle was wrapped in the fat of cow and pig. The cartridge had to be bitten off before loading it into the gun, thus Hindu and Muslim soldiers were reluctant to use it.
  • Mangal Pandey was a sepoy in the 34th Bengal Native Infantry at Barrackpore.
  • On 29th March 1857, he attacked British officers in Barrackpore.
  • He was hanged on 8th April 1857.
  • On 9th May 1857, 85 sepoys in Meerut were dismissed and sentenced to 10 years in jail for refusing to use the Enfield cartridges.
  • The Revolt of 1857 began in Meerut on 10th May, 1857 with the march towards Delhi.

Hotspots of the 1857 Revolt

  • In Delhi: Bahadur Shah Zafar II (the last Mughal ruler of India and was exiled to Rangoon, Burma (now Myanmar) after the war).
  • Actual prominent leader: General Bhakt Khan.
- Ishtahars: They glorified the co-existence of different communities under the Mughal Empire.

Leaders of 1857 Revolt

  • Delhi: General Bhakt Khan and Bahadur Shah II.
  • Lucknow: Begum Hazrat Mahal.
  • Kanpur: Nana Saheb (adopted son of Baji Rao II) / Tantia Tope.
  • Bihar: Kunwar Singh (landlord).
  • Bareilly: Bahadur Khan Rohilla.
  • Jhansi: Rani Lakshmibai → Original name: Manikarnika Tambe (Manu).
  • Faizabad: Maulvi Ahmadullah (also known as Danka Shah).
  • Uttar Pradesh: Shah Mal.
Tomb of Rani Lakshmibai is situated in Gwalior.

Suppressors of Revolt

  • Delhi: John Nicholson.
  • Lucknow: Henry Laurence.
  • Kanpur: Colin Campbell.
  • Jhansi: Hugh Rose.
  • On 20th June 1858 in Gwalior → The revolt was fully suppressed.

Aftermath of Revolt

Government of India Act 1858

  • East India Company was abolished.
  • Queen's Proclamation → Crown Rule (transfer of power from East India Company to the British Crown). Queen Victorian was the then Queen.
  • The British significantly restructured the Indian Army, and the proportion of Indian soldiers was reduced (on the recommendation of the Peel Commission).
  • Governor-General became Viceroy → 1st Viceroy: Lord Canning.

Reasons for Failure of 1857 Revolt

  • Due to limited territorial and social base, the revolt was primarily concentrated in North India.
  • Due to lack of coordination and leadership.
  • Due to lack of political perspective.

Comments

  • V D Savarkar stated it as "First war of Independence".
  • RC Majumdar: It is neither "First", nor "National" nor a "War of Independence".

Deccan Revolt (1875)

Pabna Revolt (1873-1876)

  • Started by: Ishan Chandra Roy also known as "Bidrohi Raja" or "Rebel King".

Ramosi Peasant Force (1879)

  • Founded by: Vasudeo Balwant Phadke in Maharashtra.
